tagline: Roses, rhythms, and the Black Sea
overview:
Bulgaria lies in southeastern Europe on the Balkan Peninsula, with the Danube River forming its northern border with Romania and the Black Sea washing its eastern shore. It is about the size of Tennessee. Two great mountain ranges cross the country, and between them stretch valleys of wheat, sunflowers, and roses. The capital, Sofia, sits at the foot of Vitosha Mountain, where city residents can be skiing half an hour after leaving downtown.

Around 6.5 million people live in Bulgaria, and the number has been falling as many young people move abroad for work. Bulgarian is the official language, written in the Cyrillic alphabet, which was developed by scholars in the medieval Bulgarian Empire and later spread to Russia and other Slavic lands. Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union and NATO. Its people are proud of ancient Thracian gold, Orthodox monasteries painted inside and out, and a yogurt so distinctive that a bacterium is named after the country.
landAndNature: The Balkan Mountains, called Stara Planina, run east to west across the middle of Bulgaria like a spine. To the south rise the Rila and Pirin ranges, where Musala, at 2,925 meters, is the highest peak in the whole Balkan Peninsula, and where glacial lakes lie in rocky bowls beneath ancient pine forests. Between the mountains, the Valley of the Roses fills with pink blossoms every May, harvested before dawn to make rose oil for perfumes. The Black Sea coast has long sandy beaches and warm summers, while the Danube plain has hot summers and cold, snowy winters. Brown bears, wolves, and chamois live in the mountains, and the Srebarna lake reserve on the Danube shelters rare Dalmatian pelicans.
peopleAndCulture: Most Bulgarians are Orthodox Christians, with a sizable Turkish Muslim minority and Roma communities. Meals feature shopska salad of tomatoes, cucumbers, and crumbled white cheese, banitsa pastry filled with cheese and eggs, and yogurt in nearly everything, including the cold summer soup tarator. Bulgarian folk music is famous for women's choirs singing in tight, shimmering harmonies, and for dances in uneven rhythms that are tricky even for professional musicians. On March 1 people exchange martenitsa, red-and-white yarn charms worn until the first stork or blossom of spring. Kukeri dancers in shaggy costumes and bells chase away evil spirits in winter. Wrestling, weightlifting, and rhythmic gymnastics have brought many Olympic medals, and soccer is the most popular sport.
history: The Thracians, skilled horsemen and goldsmiths, lived here in ancient times before the Romans conquered the region. In 681 Bulgars from the east joined with local Slavs to found the First Bulgarian Empire, one of Europe's oldest states. Its scholars created the Cyrillic alphabet in the 800s and 900s. The Ottoman Empire conquered Bulgaria in 1396 and ruled for nearly 500 years; an uprising in 1876 and a war between Russia and the Ottomans led to independence in 1878. Bulgaria fought on the losing side in both world wars, though it refused to deport its Jewish citizens to Nazi camps. From 1946 to 1989 it was a communist state closely tied to the Soviet Union. Democracy returned in 1990, and Bulgaria joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007.
funFacts: Bulgaria produces a large share of the world's rose oil; about 3,500 kilograms of petals go into one kilogram of oil.
The bacterium that turns milk into yogurt, Lactobacillus bulgaricus, is named after Bulgaria.
Bulgarians nod their heads to say no and shake them to say yes, confusing many visitors.
The Panagyurishte treasure, nine gold drinking vessels made by Thracians over 2,300 years ago, weighs more than six kilograms.
A recording of Bulgarian folk singing was carried into space in 1977 on the Voyager spacecraft's Golden Record.
